narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of about 5.8 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also worked against you; you ranked in the third decile compared with an average around sixth among accepted applicants. These two performance signals together created a clear picture of academic struggle that outweighed other information.

Your family income bracket was the second most influential piece of data, but it actually pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. Being in the lower-middle income group is relatively uncommon among accepted students, yet the model still saw this as a mildly positive factor.

Taken together, the model concluded your risk of failing the bar was just high enough to deny admission. To improve your chances next time, focus on raising your class standing and consider retaking the LSAT if possible, since your score of 29 sits well below the 37 average of accepted students. Strengthening these academic signals should meaningfully lower your predicted risk of failure. (248 words)
